title: Catholic: works of mercy
hook: feed the hungry, visit the sick, welcome the stranger (Matthew 25:35–36)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Hail Mary, the angel's greeting. Your line was full of grace. Did you greet someone with delight? Day two hundred sixty-five.

Picture the biggest courtroom there could ever be. Every nation gathered. A king on the throne. People are sorted to his right and his left, and they're about to learn what the whole trial was about. You'd expect the questions to be enormous. What did you believe? What did you achieve? Instead the king talks about sandwiches, and hospital visits, and a spare coat. And everyone, on both sides, is surprised. Today, on our visit to the Catholic tradition: the story behind the works of mercy.
screen: `THE BIGGEST COURTROOM.` → `WHAT WAS THE TRIAL ABOUT?` → `SANDWICHES, VISITS, A COAT.`

segments.voice: Matthew chapter twenty-five. Jesus tells of the Son of Man coming in glory to judge the nations, and the king says to those on his right, in the Douay-Rheims translation: "For I was hungry, and you gave me to eat; I was thirsty, and you gave me to drink; I was a stranger, and you took me in." Naked, and you clothed me; sick, and you visited me; in prison, and you came to me. They're confused. When did we ever see you hungry? And the king answers: "Amen I say to you, as long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me." That's the surprise. Nobody on either side knew they'd met him. He was the hungry person. The stranger. The one in the cell. Out of this passage the Catholic Church drew a list: the seven corporal works of mercy, corporal meaning of the body. Feed the hungry. Give drink to the thirsty. Clothe the naked. Shelter the homeless. Visit the sick. Visit the imprisoned. Bury the dead, that last one taken from the book of Tobit. Alongside them sit seven spiritual works of mercy, for the heart and mind: among them, comfort the sorrowful, forgive offenses, bear wrongs patiently, and pray for the living and the dead. Catholics see these not as extras for especially holy people, but as the everyday shape of faith. Mother Teresa of Calcutta, now Saint Teresa, used to count out five words on the fingers of one hand: you did it to me.
screen: `THE KING JUDGES THE NATIONS.` · `WHEN DID WE SEE YOU HUNGRY?` · `SEVEN WORKS FOR THE BODY.` · `SEVEN WORKS FOR THE HEART.` · then, large: `I WAS HUNGRY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one work of mercy for today. Sit, and go through the list slowly in your mind. Hungry. Thirsty. Without clothes, without a home. Sick. In prison. Grieving. Who near you fits one of them? A coworker who skips lunch. A friend in hospital. A neighbor who's lonely. Choose one person and one work. Picture yourself doing it. The bell holds the time.
Catholic, through the works of mercy: seven for the body, seven for the heart, from the king who says I was hungry. Today's word.
Your line: I was hungry. Today, do the one work of mercy you chose, however small, and look closely at the face in front of you. Day two hundred sixty-five.

howItsDone: Catholic parishes run food pantries, hospital and prison visits and funeral ministries as works of mercy, and many Catholics choose one work of mercy as a practice, especially during Lent.

what it means: seven works for the body and seven for the heart, as the everyday shape of Catholic faith.
what a scholar hears: six corporal works come from Matthew 25:35–36; burying the dead comes from Tobit, a book Catholics count as scripture and many Protestants don't.

notes: Douay-Rheims Matthew 25:35 and 25:40: confirm exact wording (the ending punctuation of 25:35 in particular).
Lists of the corporal and spiritual works of mercy: confirm against the Catechism.
Mother Teresa's 'five fingers, five words' (you did it to me) is widely reported; confirm or cut.
Tobit: deuterocanonical for Catholics and Orthodox, apocrypha for many Protestants; stated in trapdoor.
